title_en: Supreme People's Court Releases Typical Cases of Trademark Cases Heard by People's Courts
keywords_en: trademark rights; bankruptcy; publication of trademark cases tried by the People's Courts
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Typical Cases of Trademark Cases Heard by People's Courts Published

Case 1:

Apple Inc. v. Shenzhen Weiguan Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Ownership of "IPAD" Trademark

—— Typical Case of Major Mediation

In 2001, Shenzhen Weiguan Co., Ltd. registered the two "IPAD" trademarks in China. In August 2009, IP Company issued an offer to UK Weiguan Co., Ltd., stating its "wish to purchase all IPAD trademarks owned by Weiguan." After negotiations, on December 17, 2009, Taiwan Weiguan Co., Ltd. and IP Company signed a "Trademark Transfer Agreement" in Taiwan, transferring the IPAD trademarks, including the trademarks involved in the case, to IP Company for a consideration of 35,000 pounds. In February 2010, IP Company signed a "Rights Transfer Agreement" to transfer the two trademarks involved to Apple Inc. On April 19, 2010, Apple Inc. and IP Company filed a lawsuit with the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province against Shenzhen Weiguan Co., Ltd., seeking an order based on the trademark transfer agreement signed between Taiwan Weiguan Co., Ltd. and IP Company to declare that the two "IPAD" trademarks owned by Shenzhen Weiguan Co., Ltd. in China belonged to them.

After trial, the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province held that the trademark transfer agreement was signed by Taiwan Weiguan Co., Ltd., was not binding on Shenzhen Weiguan Co., Ltd., and did not constitute apparent agency, and thus dismissed the claims of Apple Inc. et al. Apple Inc. and IP Company appealed to the Guangdong High People's Court. During the second instance, the Guangdong High People's Court, after multiple mediations, finally reached a mediation agreement between the parties in June 2012, whereby Apple Inc. paid USD 60 million and Weiguan Co., Ltd. transferred the "IPAD" trademarks involved to Apple Inc. The mediation agreement has been executed.

As Weiguan Co., Ltd. was on the verge of bankruptcy at the time of the lawsuit, the "IPAD" trademarks involved were subject to sequential seizure by several banks. The handling of the case involved multiple interests and attracted significant domestic and international attention. The settlement through mediation maximized the value of the IPAD trademarks, effectively protected the rights of creditors, explored a new path for resolving disputes over the ownership of foreign-related trademark rights, and achieved good legal and social effects.

Case 2:

Bestseller Co., Ltd. v. Cui Huansuo et al. — Civil Dispute over Infringement of "Jack Jones" Trademark

—— Typical Civil Dispute Case of Trademark Infringement Involving the Internet

Plaintiff Bestseller Co., Ltd. was authorized to use the "JACK&JONES" trademark and to file infringement lawsuits in China, and was registered to have exclusive rights to the "Jack Jones" trademark. Defendants Cui Huansuo and Du Xinghua, without authorization, registered the domain name ackonescn.net and used it to set up the Jack Jones Chinese website. The search result page title of the website displayed "JACKJONES Chinese Website - Jack Jones Chinese Website - JACK&JONES Official Chinese Website"; the page description used expressions such as "Jack Jones Chinese" and "Jack Jones Official Website"; the homepage and related pages extensively used expressions such as "Jack Jones Chinese Website" and "ackones Chinese Website" as well as the Jack Jones and logo marks, accompanied by content such as "Introduction to Jack Jones"; the source files of relevant web pages extensively used text related to Jack Jones, JACKJONES, ackones, etc.; each piece of clothing listed under the "Clothing Directory" had a corresponding actual sample image and the Jack Jones and logo mark on the left; the clothing sold used packaging printed with the Jack Jones and logo mark, and the clothing labels and hangtags bore the Jack Jones and logo mark, with buttons and cufflinks marked "JACK&JONES," and the certificate of quality indicated the trademark as "Jack Jones," etc. Bestseller Co., Ltd. believed the defendants' actions infringed its exclusive right to use the registered trademark and filed a lawsuit with the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing, requesting an order for the defendants to cease infringement, eliminate adverse effects, and compensate for losses.

After trial, the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing held that the defendants' actions constituted, without the trademark owner's permission, using trademarks identical or similar to "JACK&JONES" and "Jack Jones" in the promotion, introduction, and transaction of identical goods, and selling goods infringing the exclusive rights to the above trademarks, which could cause the relevant public to mistakenly believe that the owner of the domain name, website, and provider of the clothing were Bestseller Co., Ltd., thereby constituting infringement on Bestseller Co., Ltd.'s lawful rights. Therefore, on April 26, 2011, the court ordered the two defendants to cease selling infringing clothing, close the website involved used for selling infringing clothing, cease using the domain name ackonescn.net involved (which was to be registered and used by the plaintiff), and ordered the two defendants to publish statements in the Legal Daily and on Sina.com (www.sina.com.cn) to eliminate adverse effects, and to compensate the plaintiff for economic losses and reasonable litigation expenses of nearly RMB 2 million.

This case is a relatively typical dispute over trademark infringement involving the Internet. The defendants engaged in a series of acts infringing trademark rights, with an obvious intention to ride on the coattails of a well-known brand. Considering the defendants' obvious subjective malice and the serious consequences of the infringement, the court supported most of the plaintiff's claims, effectively cracking down on the infringement.

Case 3:

Gap Co., Ltd. v. Xinhengli Co., Ltd. — Administrative Dispute over Opposition to "GAP" Trademark

—— Typical Case of Administrative Dispute over Malicious Registration of a Trademark

In July 1992, Gap Co., Ltd. obtained registration of the "GAP" trademark (the cited trademark) for goods in Class 25 (shirts, T-shirts) and Class 18 (backpacks, etc.). On April 19, 1999, Xinhengli Co., Ltd. applied for registration of the "GAP" trademark (the opposed trademark) for goods in Class 9 (eyeglasses, etc.), and Gap Co., Ltd. filed an opposition. The Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board (TRAB) held that the goods designated by the opposed trademark and the goods and services designated by the cited trademark differed in function, purpose, and the method and object of service, and did not constitute similar goods or services using similar trademarks, and therefore ruled that the opposed trademark should be approved for registration.

Gap Co., Ltd., dissatisfied, filed suit with the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court. The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court, after trial, upheld the ruling of the TRAB. Gap Co., Ltd., dissatisfied, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court. The Beijing High People's Court also upheld the first-instance judgment. Gap Co., Ltd., dissatisfied, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. After review, the Supreme People's Court issued a ruling to take the case for retrial and rendered a final judgment on March 31, 2012. The court held: The evidence submitted by Gap Co., Ltd. could prove that its "GAP" series trademarks had been used and had gained a certain degree of fame in China before the application date of the opposed trademark. Moreover, from Xinhengli Co., Ltd.'s claim that it originated from the United States, its flaunting of characteristics identical to "GAP" clothing, and its actual use, it was evident that Xinhengli Co., Ltd. was aware of the fame of the cited trademark and had the subjective intent to ride on the coattails of the "GAP" brand. Although the goods designated by the opposed trademark, such as "sunglasses, eyeglass frames," were classified in different major classes under the "Classification of Similar Goods and Services" from the goods primarily designated by the cited trademark, such as "clothing," the functions, purposes, sales channels, and consumer groups of the goods were significantly related. Especially for fashion brands, it is common for a company to operate both clothing and accessories such as eyewear under the same brand. Considering the certain fame of the cited trademark, the applicant's intent to free-ride on the opposed trademark, the substantial identity of the opposed trademark with the cited trademark, and their respective use on goods such as eyewear and clothing, it was objectively likely to cause the relevant public to believe that the goods were provided by the same entity or that there was a specific connection between the providers. Therefore, the opposed trademark and the cited trademark had constituted similar trademarks used on similar goods and should not be approved for registration. Accordingly, the Supreme People's Court annulled the ruling of the TRAB and the first and second instance judgments, and ordered the TRAB to make a new ruling.

This case is a relatively typical case of malicious trademark registration. The TRAB and the first and second instance courts approved the registration of the opposed trademark on the grounds that the goods for which the opposed trademark was used were not similar to those for which the cited trademark was used. The Supreme People's Court, considering that the applicant for the opposed trademark was aware of the fame of the cited trademark, had an obvious intent to free-ride in applying for the opposed trademark, and that clothing and eyewear had a certain degree of relevance, ultimately ruled that the opposed trademark should not be approved for registration, demonstrating the judicial orientation and attitude of the people's courts in curbing malicious trademark registration in accordance with the law.
